name: London
title: A crossing became a crossroads.
deck: The Thames offered a route for boats—and a place where land routes could meet.
question: Which combination helped Roman London develop here?
options: A Thames crossing and access to river trade
A nearby source of Alpine glacier ice
A harbour directly on the open Mediterranean

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Water brought opportunity.
steps.text: The Thames connected the settlement with a wider river and sea network. A crossing also allowed people and goods to move between its banks.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: A bridge made a meeting point.
steps.text: The Romans established Londinium and built a timber bridge early in its history. Roads, waterfront activity, and the settlement developed around this connection.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful river needs managing.
steps.text: A river is an opportunity and a constraint. Building beside tidal water requires crossings, working waterfronts, and continuing decisions about how people use its banks.

takeaway: The river offered possibilities. People turned them into a city.

name: Venice
title: A city learned to live between land and water.
deck: Islands in a shallow lagoon became the setting for a distinctive maritime city.
question: What most directly shaped Venice’s urban form?
options: A continuous mountain ridge through its centre
Its islands, tidal channels, and lagoon setting
A broad desert plain without surface water

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: A different kind of ground.
steps.text: The lagoon offered islands and channels rather than a simple continuous building site. Water influenced where settlements could grow and how people moved.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: Adaptation became an identity.
steps.text: People connected islands, developed waterways, and adapted buildings to the setting. Over centuries, this became a city whose streets and maritime connections worked together.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: The setting needs constant care.
steps.text: Venice and its lagoon remain interdependent. High water and changes to the lagoon environment pose challenges to buildings, habitats, and the city’s future.

takeaway: Venice’s setting was neither effortless nor inevitable. Its cityscape records centuries of adaptation.

name: Singapore
title: A small island sits on a very large network.
deck: Singapore’s location places it near major maritime routes between oceans.
question: Which geographical advantage helped Singapore become a trading hub?
options: A location on major maritime trade routes
A navigable river connecting it directly to Europe
Its position inside an inland mountain basin

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Look beyond the island.
steps.text: Singapore sits at a maritime crossroads in Southeast Asia. Its importance becomes clearer when viewed as part of a network of routes rather than by land area alone.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: Location needed investment.
steps.text: Port infrastructure, services, connectivity, and policy helped turn a strategic position into a major maritime hub. Geography supplied an opportunity, not a finished outcome.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: Connection creates dependence.
steps.text: A hub gains from international movement but must continually adapt its infrastructure and services. Ships do not choose a port merely because a map places it nearby.

takeaway: A good location becomes valuable through the connections people build around it.

name: Istanbul
title: A narrow passage made a powerful position.
deck: The Bosphorus places Istanbul between major land regions and connected seas.
question: What makes Istanbul’s location strategically important?
options: Its isolation from all navigable water
Its position beside the Bosphorus between land regions and sea routes
Its location at the source of the Amazon

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Water narrows. Routes meet.
steps.text: The Bosphorus connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Marmara and onward toward the Mediterranean. The city occupies a meeting point between the Balkans and Anatolia.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: A position became a capital.
steps.text: Successive societies built on this strategic setting. Istanbul’s history includes its roles as a capital of the Eastern Roman and Ottoman empires.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A connection is also a division.
steps.text: Waterways offer access while separating shores. A city in this setting has to organise movement across land and water as well as benefit from the routes passing through.

takeaway: The same strait that divides shores can make a city a meeting place.

name: Cusco
title: A high valley became an imperial centre.
deck: Cusco’s setting combines mountain terrain, rivers, and a fertile alluvial valley.
question: What geographical setting supported Cusco’s development?
options: A low-lying tropical coastal delta
An island at the mouth of the Rhine
A fertile, river-fed valley in the Andes

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: A valley within the mountains.
steps.text: Cusco lies high in the Peruvian Andes in a fertile alluvial valley fed by several rivers. This was a setting where mountain terrain and usable valley land came together.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: Political decisions shaped the city.
steps.text: Inca rulers developed Cusco into a complex capital with administrative and religious functions. Its significance depended on institutions and power as well as its physical setting.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A city carries layers of history.
steps.text: Following Spanish conquest, buildings were erected over and around Inca structures. The city’s present form records both its Andean setting and major changes in political control.

takeaway: Terrain helps explain a setting. Human decisions explain much of what happened there.

name: Paris
title: A river gave the city a spine.
deck: The Seine helped organise movement, crossings, and the shape of Paris.
question: Which feature has strongly structured Paris’s urban landscape?
options: The Seine and the connections across its banks
A natural harbour on the Pacific
A ring of active volcanoes

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: A bend with connections.
steps.text: Paris developed along the Seine, within a larger network of rivers in the Paris Basin. Its banks and islands formed a setting for settlement and movement.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: Bridges joined more than banks.
steps.text: Successive communities and rulers built crossings, quays, monuments, and neighbourhoods around the river. The resulting cityscape records centuries of decisions rather than a single founding plan.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: The banks remain contested space.
steps.text: Transport, public access, building, and heritage protection compete along a limited waterfront. The river continues to influence how the city changes.

takeaway: A city’s river can remain its organising thread long after its first settlements.

source.name: UNESCO · Paris, Banks of the Seine

name: Rome
title: A riverside setting became a centre of power.
deck: Rome’s physical setting combines the Tiber with a complex landscape of hills.
question: Which river is central to Rome’s geographical setting?
options: The Seine
The Tiber
The Danube

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Water beside higher ground.
steps.text: Rome developed on the banks of the Tiber within an uneven landscape. The river was a geographical connection, while the surrounding terrain shaped how areas of the city related to one another.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: Institutions expanded the setting.
steps.text: Political power, engineering, and successive building programmes transformed a settlement into a major centre. The republic, empire, and later city each added layers.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: Later cities inherit earlier ones.
steps.text: Rome’s streets and buildings occupy a landscape already reshaped many times. Preserving older layers while accommodating current needs remains part of urban life.

takeaway: The Tiber helps explain the setting; centuries of human decisions explain the city.

name: Lyon
title: Two rivers made one distinctive setting.
deck: Lyon occupies a meeting point of the Rhône and Saône, with hills rising nearby.
question: What is a defining feature of Lyon’s location?
options: An isolated island in the Atlantic
A dry basin with no rivers
The confluence of the Rhône and Saône

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Two waterways meet.
steps.text: The Rhône and Saône come together at Lyon. The rivers and nearby hills created distinct areas of usable ground and different routes through the landscape.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: A city grew in stages.
steps.text: From its Roman history onward, Lyon developed through successive urban expansions. Neighbourhoods, crossings, and commercial activity gave the river setting different roles over time.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: Water divides as well as connects.
steps.text: River corridors require bridges and careful planning. The land between waterways is valuable, but it is not unlimited or separate from the rivers around it.

takeaway: A confluence can connect routes while giving a city a very particular shape.

name: Prague
title: A river linked a city of different heights.
deck: The Vltava and Prague’s terrain helped shape a city on both banks.
question: Which physical feature connects Prague’s historic districts?
options: The Vltava River and its crossings
An inland salt lake
A desert caravan oasis

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Banks with different perspectives.
steps.text: Prague’s historic centre occupies both sides of the Vltava. The river and changes in elevation contribute to the relationship between its districts and landmarks.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: Crossings became civic places.
steps.text: Building bridges connected areas that water separated. Rulers, merchants, religious communities, and residents added to a cityscape whose history is visible across the river.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A living city is also a heritage landscape.
steps.text: New development and transport needs must coexist with the historic river setting. Preserving the relationship between buildings, views, and open spaces requires active choices.

takeaway: A bridge can be both infrastructure and a way of understanding a city.

name: Budapest
title: Different riverbanks became a shared cityscape.
deck: Buda’s higher ground and Pest’s plain meet across the Danube.
question: What helps explain the contrasting landscapes of Buda and Pest?
options: Both sit on identical volcanic islands
Buda’s higher right bank faces Pest’s flatter left bank
A mountain range separates them from the Danube

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: One river, contrasting sides.
steps.text: The Danube runs between the higher ground associated with Buda and the plain associated with Pest. This contrast is central to the historic cityscape.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: Connections joined urban histories.
steps.text: Settlement, institutions, bridges, and building linked areas with different histories and physical forms. The river became a shared urban frontage rather than merely an edge.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: Keep the relationship visible.
steps.text: Development on either bank can affect the wider river panorama. The heritage value lies partly in the relationship between terrain, water, and buildings—not just isolated monuments.

takeaway: One city can make sense only when you look at both sides of its river.

source.name: UNESCO · Budapest and the Banks of the Danube

name: Amsterdam
title: Managing water helped create urban space.
deck: The Amstel, the IJ, and an engineered canal network shaped Amsterdam.
question: What was central to Amsterdam’s historic expansion?
options: Building only on a steep mountain ridge
Removing every connection with navigable water
Organising water, canals, and reclaimed urban land

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: A lowland meeting of waters.
steps.text: The confluence of the Amstel and the IJ provided the setting for Amsterdam’s founding port. Water connections offered opportunity within a landscape that needed management.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: Canals were a city-making project.
steps.text: Later expansion used a planned canal network and new urban land. This connected transport, water engineering, property development, and the organisation of neighbourhoods.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: The system needs care.
steps.text: An engineered water city depends on continued management. Canals are part of the urban structure, not decoration that can be considered separately from buildings and movement.

takeaway: Sometimes the setting of a city is partly built, not simply found.

name: Rotterdam
title: A river settlement learned to reach the sea.
deck: Rotterdam’s history connects a dam in the Rotte with a much larger port landscape.
question: What combination helps explain Rotterdam’s development?
options: A river setting followed by major investment in port access
A location in an isolated alpine valley
A port created without any navigable water

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: A lowland river setting.
steps.text: Rotterdam grew around a dam in the Rotte within the wider waterways of the Rhine–Meuse region. Inland and maritime connections made the setting significant.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: Access had to be maintained.
steps.text: Port growth required infrastructure and changing connections with the sea. The city archive describes nineteenth-century concern about the port silting up.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful position is not enough.
steps.text: A port must adapt when channels, ships, and economic demands change. Engineering and investment help determine whether geographical access remains commercially useful.

takeaway: A port’s geography is an ongoing project, not a permanent guarantee.

name: Lisbon
title: A river opens toward an ocean.
deck: Lisbon sits beside the Tagus estuary, with access to Atlantic routes.
question: Which water setting helps explain Lisbon’s maritime connections?
options: A closed lake with no outlet
The Tagus estuary and its Atlantic access
A river flowing directly to the Arctic Ocean

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: A broad water gateway.
steps.text: The Tagus reaches a wide estuary beside Lisbon before meeting the Atlantic. River and maritime settings come together here.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: A waterfront became infrastructure.
steps.text: Port facilities, navigation channels, and land transport connections make the estuary useful for moving goods and people. Access depends on organisation as well as water.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: Many uses share the estuary.
steps.text: Navigation, urban life, recreation, and natural habitats occupy the same broader setting. Decisions about the waterfront affect more than the ships arriving there.

takeaway: An estuary links inland geography with ocean networks.

name: New York City
title: A harbour became an urban gateway.
deck: New York’s waterfront connects a large estuary with ocean commerce.
question: What has helped keep New York’s harbour useful for shipping?
options: Being an inland mountain lake
Having no rivers or deposited sediment
Natural access combined with maintained navigation channels

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: An estuary at the coast.
steps.text: New York and New Jersey share a harbour system connected with rivers and the Atlantic. This offers a large water-based setting for urban activity.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: The gateway was developed.
steps.text: Shipping facilities and navigation works helped turn this setting into an active port. Trade and settlement reshaped shorelines and water spaces over time.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: Channels do not maintain themselves.
steps.text: Sediment accumulates in estuaries. The US Army Corps of Engineers describes dredging as necessary to remove shoals that interfere with navigation.

takeaway: A natural harbour can still depend on very deliberate engineering.

source.name: US Army Corps of Engineers · New York harbour navigation

name: Sydney
title: A sheltered cove changed a colonial plan.
deck: Sydney’s colonial settlement began at Sydney Cove within Port Jackson.
question: Where did the First Fleet establish its settlement after finding Botany Bay unsuitable?
options: Sydney Cove in Port Jackson
An inland site beside Lake Eyre
A settlement on the opposite side of Australia

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: A cove within a harbour.
steps.text: Port Jackson offered the water setting in which Sydney Cove was chosen for British settlement. The choice followed the fleet’s initial arrival at Botany Bay.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: A decision with lasting effects.
steps.text: The colonial settlement established in 1788 developed into the city of Sydney. This was not an empty landscape: Aboriginal communities had lived in the region long before the fleet arrived.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: Access did not mean absence of consequences.
steps.text: The harbour story includes colonial institutions and their impact on existing peoples. Explaining a location should not turn settlement into an inevitable or uncomplicated outcome.

takeaway: A geographical advantage can sit within a much more difficult human history.

source.name: Parliament of New South Wales · Early European settlement

name: Hong Kong
title: A harbour connected a city with global trade.
deck: Hong Kong’s port has long been central to its development and prosperity.
question: Which combination helps explain Hong Kong’s port role?
options: An isolated inland basin
A strategic maritime location and developed port facilities
A location without access to regional markets

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Position within a trading region.
steps.text: Hong Kong lies on major Far East trade routes within the Asia-Pacific region. Its harbour setting helped give maritime activity a central place in the city.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: Facilities made location useful.
steps.text: Terminals, shipping services, and connections with surrounding markets developed around that setting. The port’s role rests on a working system rather than location alone.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: Waterfront space has competing demands.
steps.text: Shipping, urban development, passenger travel, and other activities share a constrained coastal environment. A successful harbour has to be managed as well as occupied.

takeaway: The value of a harbour comes from both its setting and its connections.

source.name: Hong Kong Marine Department · The Port

name: Cape Town
title: A stopping place became a colonial city.
deck: Table Bay sat along the sea route linking Europe with Asia around southern Africa.
question: Why did the Dutch East India Company establish a station at the Cape?
options: To build an inland canal to the Mediterranean
To grow crops beneath Antarctic ice
To supply passing ships with water and fresh produce

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: A strategic pause in a long voyage.
steps.text: The Cape occupied an important position on ocean routes around southern Africa. Ships on lengthy voyages needed opportunities to obtain supplies.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: A station grew into something larger.
steps.text: The Dutch East India Company established a refreshment station in 1652, with gardens and fortifications serving commercial and strategic purposes.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: The place already had inhabitants.
steps.text: Khoi communities used the Table Bay region before the colonial station. The city’s growth therefore belongs to a history of contact, dispossession, and unequal power as well as maritime geography.

takeaway: A convenient stopping place can become the beginning of a much larger transformation.

source.name: City of Cape Town · City Hall and precinct history

name: Mumbai
title: A safe anchorage became a maritime city.
deck: Mumbai’s harbour offered advantages for shipping along India’s western seaboard.
question: Which feature attracted maritime interest in Mumbai’s setting?
options: Its sheltered natural harbour
Its location at the source of the Ganges
Its position beyond all ocean trade routes

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: A haven for vessels.
steps.text: Mumbai’s natural harbour offered a maritime base on India’s western coast. Its advantages were recognised long before the modern port took its present form.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: Commerce changed the scale.
steps.text: Port development and connections with wider trade turned a geographical opportunity into a major commercial system. Political control and investment shaped that transformation.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: The port and city share a shore.
steps.text: A growing maritime city must organise the space needed by shipping alongside other urban uses. The historical harbour cannot explain today’s metropolis without its later infrastructure and institutions.

takeaway: A sheltered anchorage is a beginning, not a complete explanation for a metropolis.

name: Rio de Janeiro
title: A city fitted itself between mountains and sea.
deck: Rio’s landscape combines Guanabara Bay, the Atlantic coast, and steep forested terrain.
question: What strongly shapes Rio de Janeiro’s physical layout?
options: An uninterrupted flat desert
The interaction of mountains, bay, and ocean
A broad inland ice sheet

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Space between rising ground and water.
steps.text: Rio occupies coastal land framed by Guanabara Bay and steep mountains. This creates dramatic contrasts over short distances.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: Building worked with and changed the setting.
steps.text: Neighbourhoods, designed landscapes, routes, and public spaces developed within this terrain. The city’s identity comes from interaction between natural features and human activity.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: The landscape is part of the city.
steps.text: Mountains, forests, shorelines, and urban areas are interdependent. Protecting the cultural landscape means considering their relationships rather than treating nature as a backdrop.

takeaway: A skyline can be shaped as much by the land around buildings as by the buildings themselves.

source.name: UNESCO · Rio de Janeiro, Carioca Landscapes

name: San Francisco
title: Ships helped turn a port into a boomtown.
deck: San Francisco’s bay-side settlement expanded rapidly during the Gold Rush.
question: What helped drive the surge of ships and people into San Francisco in the mid-nineteenth century?
options: A newly completed canal to the Nile
The closure of every Pacific shipping route
The California Gold Rush

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: A cove connected with a larger bay.
steps.text: The settlement’s waterfront offered a place for ships to arrive within the San Francisco Bay system.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: Opportunity drew a sudden crowd.
steps.text: Gold Rush migration brought vessels and people in extraordinary numbers. Some ships were abandoned, reused, or incorporated into the expanding waterfront.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: Growth changed the shoreline.
steps.text: Later building and fill buried parts of the maritime landscape. The ships preserved beneath modern streets reveal how quickly people can remake a coastal setting.

takeaway: An urban street can conceal the waterfront that helped create it.

source.name: National Park Service · Buried ships of San Francisco

name: Buenos Aires
title: A port connected an interior with wider markets.
deck: Buenos Aires developed beside the Río de la Plata, with links extending inland.
question: What became a major strength of Buenos Aires as a commercial centre?
options: Its port and connections with interior cities
An isolated location without navigable water
A harbour on the Pacific side of the Andes

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: A broad estuary setting.
steps.text: Buenos Aires sits beside the Río de la Plata on South America’s Atlantic side. The setting offered a water-based gateway rather than a position within the Andes.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: Political status and trade reinforced one another.
steps.text: Its role as a colonial capital strengthened its commercial position. The city’s official history identifies its port and inland connections as major advantages.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: Access had to be built.
steps.text: Port infrastructure and waterfront development changed the city’s relationship with the estuary. The usefulness of a broad expanse of water still depended on practical ways to handle ships and cargo.

takeaway: A gateway matters because of what lies behind it as well as beyond it.

source.name: City of Buenos Aires · City history

name: Shanghai
title: A river city grew into a coastal port network.
deck: Shanghai’s port geography connects the Huangpu with the Yangtze Delta and the sea.
question: What helps explain Shanghai’s maritime position?
options: A closed mountain basin far from rivers
Connections between river transport, delta land, and sea routes
A location on the Atlantic coast

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Rivers connect with the coast.
steps.text: The Huangpu meets the Yangtze in a broader delta region linked with the sea. This offers more than a single waterfront: it connects different scales of transport.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: The port moved and expanded.
steps.text: As shipping needs changed, terminals and port functions developed beyond the historic riverfront. Modernisation reshaped the geography of the port.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A hub has to keep adapting.
steps.text: Larger ships, cargo systems, land requirements, and regional connections affect where port activity can operate. The original waterfront is only one part of the modern system.

takeaway: A city’s working geography can expand far beyond its most photographed riverbank.

source.name: OECD · The competitiveness of global port-cities: Shanghai

name: Cairo
title: A river corridor became a setting for a capital.
deck: Cairo occupies a strategic position beside the Nile near the approach to its delta.
question: Which geographical setting is central to Cairo’s location?
options: An island in the Indian Ocean
A highland valley in the Andes
The Nile corridor near its delta region

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Water within a much drier region.
steps.text: The Nile creates a major inhabited corridor through Egypt. Cairo’s setting lies beside the river near the transition toward the delta.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: Political and religious roles reinforced the setting.
steps.text: Successive urban centres and institutions developed in this region. Cairo became a major political and religious centre rather than simply a settlement beside water.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A capital concentrates demands.
steps.text: People, administration, movement, and development place overlapping demands on a limited river setting. Geography offers a framework, but political decisions help determine where activity concentrates.

takeaway: A river helps explain where a city can thrive; institutions help explain why it becomes a capital.

name: Kathmandu
title: A valley holds more than one urban story.
deck: Kathmandu belongs to a wider valley of historic cities, settlements, and religious places.
question: What setting helps explain Kathmandu’s relationship with nearby historic centres?
options: A shared valley containing several connected settlements
A line of isolated coral atolls
A river delta on the Mediterranean

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: A valley within a mountain region.
steps.text: Kathmandu is part of a wider valley landscape rather than a solitary settlement on a summit.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: Several centres shaped the region.
steps.text: Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur developed distinctive urban and cultural roles. Palaces, public spaces, shrines, and local communities gave the valley a network of centres.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: The wider setting matters.
steps.text: Heritage places sit within living urban environments. Caring for the valley requires attention to settlements and communities as well as its best-known monuments.

takeaway: A capital can be understood better as part of a regional network than as one point on a map.

name: Mexico City
title: A modern city carries the memory of a lake.
deck: Mexico City grew over the island city of Tenochtitlan and a transformed lake landscape.
question: What was a defining part of Tenochtitlan’s setting?
options: An Atlantic cliff-top harbour
An island city within a lake system
A settlement on an Antarctic ice shelf

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Water once framed the city.
steps.text: Tenochtitlan developed as an island city within a lake landscape. Its setting differs greatly from the continuous urban fabric visible today.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: Conquest changed the landscape.
steps.text: After Spanish conquest, the colonial city was built over the older capital. Drainage transformed the surrounding lake environment as the city changed.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: The past remains part of the present.
steps.text: The modern city occupies a landscape reshaped by successive societies. Understanding its setting requires looking beneath today’s streets to the earlier relationship between land and water.

takeaway: A city can outgrow the visible landscape that first made its location distinctive.

source.name: UNESCO · Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco

name: Québec City
title: A city rose above a river gateway.
deck: A cliff and a major river helped shape two connected levels of settlement.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Québec City’s story?
options: A cliff overlooking the St Lawrence
A volcanic crater in the Pacific
A landlocked desert oasis

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: The St Lawrence offered access inland and towards the Atlantic. The cliff separated an upper site from the waterfront below.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: French colonial settlement developed an administrative and defensive Upper Town alongside the trading activity of the Lower Town. Fortifications reinforced the distinction.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: A commanding height also creates steep journeys. Connections between the two levels remain part of the city’s everyday geography.

takeaway: Height and water played different roles in the same city.

name: Edinburgh
title: A fortress gave a ridge its direction.
deck: Edinburgh’s contrasting old and new districts reveal two ways of building a capital.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Edinburgh’s story?
options: A town built entirely on floating islands
A ridge dominated by a fortress
An unbroken flat grid from its beginnings

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: Castle Rock stands above surrounding low ground. The Old Town stretches along a ridge, giving its streets a strong direction.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: A medieval settlement grew beneath the fortress. From the eighteenth century, the planned New Town offered a contrasting street pattern beyond the old core.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: Expanding beyond a constrained ridge created more room, but joining old and new districts required crossings and changes of level.

takeaway: Edinburgh’s contrast comes from different planning choices on different ground.

name: Porto
title: A river valley opened towards the sea.
deck: Porto climbs the banks of the Douro close to its Atlantic outlet.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Porto’s story?
options: The source of the Amazon
An inland salt lake
The Douro near its Atlantic outlet

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: Steep riverbanks place the waterfront and higher neighbourhoods at different levels. The Douro connects the city with an inland valley and the ocean beyond.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: Port activity and centuries of construction created a dense hillside city. Bridges connected the two banks rather than removing their differences in height.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: The dramatic setting also makes movement demanding. Routes must negotiate slopes, bridge approaches, and a busy river edge.

takeaway: Porto’s river is both a connection and a change of level.

name: Salzburg
title: A valley became a stage for power.
deck: River, hills, and centuries of patronage shaped Salzburg’s compact historic centre.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Salzburg’s story?
options: A river valley framed by hills
An Arctic ice shelf
A chain of coral atolls

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: The Salzach runs between hills that frame the old city. The setting concentrates routes and creates a striking contrast between the valley floor and higher ground.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: Prince-archbishops shaped a city-state here. Religious buildings, public spaces, and work by Italian architects gave the historic centre much of its Baroque character.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: A confined setting leaves limited room for new construction. Maintaining the relationship between buildings, hills, and river matters as much as preserving individual monuments.

takeaway: Landscape framed Salzburg; political and artistic choices composed the city.

name: Bern
title: A bend in the river became a city’s outline.
deck: Bern’s old town occupies raised ground embraced by the Aare.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Bern’s story?
options: The mouth of the Nile
A loop of the Aare
A Mediterranean island

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: The Aare curves around the old city, creating a distinct peninsula-like site. Water and slopes define its edges rather than a regular rectangular boundary.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: Founded in the twelfth century, Bern developed a remarkably coherent street pattern. Arcades, fountains, and successive rebuilding added layers within that framework.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: A river loop provides a clear edge but limits connections. Bridges let the city expand beyond a site that could not simply widen in every direction.

takeaway: A natural boundary can shape a city long after it grows beyond it.

name: Regensburg
title: A bridge tied a trading city together.
deck: Regensburg’s medieval streets still meet a major European river.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Regensburg’s story?
options: A harbour on the Red Sea
A mountain pass above permanent glaciers
A Danube crossing and trading connections

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: The Danube connected settlements along its course. A crossing linked its banks and brought overland movement into contact with river traffic.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: Regensburg became a medieval trading centre. Its twelfth-century Stone Bridge joined the city with Stadtamhof, while merchants built the houses and towers still visible in the old town.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: A useful crossing attracts activity to a concentrated place. Keeping historic streets and a river crossing usable requires balancing access with conservation.

takeaway: A bridge is infrastructure, but it can also become a city’s organising idea.

name: Bamberg
title: One town grew in several landscapes.
deck: Bamberg joins hilltop institutions, river channels, and lower working districts.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Bamberg’s story?
options: Hills, river branches, and distinct urban districts
A single artificial island in open ocean
A settlement without any waterways

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: Hills and branches of the Regnitz give Bamberg more than one kind of urban ground. Higher sites and waterside areas offered different possibilities.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: Religious and political institutions occupied prominent sites, while the island town and gardening district developed other patterns of work and settlement. These parts formed a connected historic town.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: Preserving Bamberg means caring for relationships between districts, not just a single skyline. Waterways, productive land, and old streets all belong to the story.

takeaway: Different kinds of ground can support different parts of the same city.

name: Bruges
title: Waterways helped a town face the world.
deck: Bruges turned commercial connections into a rich medieval cityscape.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Bruges’s story?
options: A permanent polar sea-ice route
Waterway connections and medieval trade
A city founded at the summit of the Alps

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: Waterways linked the town with a wider coastal trading region. Its canals were part of a changing system of access, not evidence that the city stood directly on the open sea.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: Medieval merchants and civic institutions built an influential commercial centre. The wealth of trade helped support public buildings, domestic architecture, and artistic exchange.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: Water connections change over time. Maintaining a historic trading town today involves preserving canals and streets whose functions have evolved.

takeaway: Commercial reach can be much larger than the town that anchors it.

name: Galle
title: Fortifications followed the rock.
deck: Galle’s old town adapted European plans to a South Asian coastal site.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Galle’s story?
options: A plateau surrounded by desert dunes
A town constructed on seasonal sea ice
A rocky coastal promontory

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: A rocky promontory projects into the sea on Sri Lanka’s southwest coast. Its shape gave builders a defined waterfront site rather than a blank geometric canvas.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: Portuguese and later Dutch colonial authorities fortified the town. Local craftspeople adapted buildings to the climate, while ramparts followed the terrain and a street grid organised the interior.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: The fort remains a living place. New uses and modern services must fit streets, homes, and defences shaped for earlier needs.

takeaway: Galle shows how an imported plan changes when it meets a particular place.

name: Tallinn
title: A hilltop stronghold met a merchant town.
deck: Tallinn’s historic centre records both authority and Baltic commercial connections.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Tallinn’s story?
options: A fortified hill and Baltic trading connections
An equatorial rainforest river delta
A town entirely below the ocean floor

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: A coastal setting offered maritime access, while Toompea provided elevated ground beside the lower town. The two areas did not serve identical functions.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: A fortified upper centre and a lower merchant town developed together. Membership in the Hanseatic trading network helped support the churches, public buildings, and merchants’ houses that survive.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: Different districts left different street patterns and views. Keeping those relationships legible matters as the modern city grows around them.

takeaway: Tallinn’s old town connects two kinds of power: the stronghold and the marketplace.

name: Riga
title: A river helped connect a trading region.
deck: Riga’s old centre and later districts reveal successive waves of commercial growth.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Riga’s story?
options: A lake at the South Pole
The Daugava and Baltic trading routes
A pass through the Andes

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: The Daugava reaches towards the Gulf of Riga, connecting inland routes with the Baltic region. The riverfront gave the city a strong axis.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: Medieval Hanseatic trade supported Riga’s prosperity. Later economic growth expanded the city beyond its medieval core, leaving wooden suburbs and extensive Art Nouveau architecture.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: A city can outgrow its original centre without losing it. The challenge is to connect later districts while retaining their different scales and character.

takeaway: Riga’s neighbourhoods record how a trading city expanded through time.

name: Dubrovnik
title: A compact city looked out to sea.
deck: Dubrovnik’s walls enclosed a city whose connections extended far beyond them.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Dubrovnik’s story?
options: An inland glacier-fed salt flat
The headwaters of the Mississippi
Access to Adriatic maritime routes

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: A coastal site on the Adriatic placed the town beside Mediterranean sea routes. Its enclosed urban core contrasts with the open water beyond.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: Dubrovnik developed into an important maritime power. Walls, civic buildings, and religious institutions gave physical form to a city shaped by commerce and political organisation.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: Earthquake and war damaged the city at different times. Its continued existence reflects restoration and collective choices, not the permanence of stone alone.

takeaway: The walls define a small place; its maritime history reaches much farther.

name: Split
title: A palace became part of a living city.
deck: Split’s historic core grew through the reuse of a Roman imperial complex.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Split’s story?
options: The reuse of Diocletian’s Palace
A completely untouched empty palace
A medieval city built on an ice sheet

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: A coastal site offered an outward connection to the Adriatic. Within it, a large Roman palace created a powerful built framework for later settlement.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: People adapted Diocletian’s Palace over centuries. Churches, homes, streets, and later buildings became interwoven with ancient structures rather than replacing the complex with an empty monument.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: Living inside inherited architecture creates difficult choices. Homes and everyday services must coexist with structures valued for their long history.

takeaway: Sometimes the most important landscape a city inherits is already built.

name: Kotor
title: A harbour nestled beneath steep slopes.
deck: Kotor’s natural setting brings sheltered water and mountains unusually close together.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Kotor’s story?
options: A plain thousands of kilometres from any sea
A natural harbour beneath steep mountain slopes
A settlement on an active floating iceberg

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: The inner Bay of Kotor offers a harbour backed by steep terrain. The narrow strip between shore and slope concentrates buildings and movement.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: The medieval town became an artistic and commercial centre. Its walls and buildings connected maritime activity with a defensible settlement at the foot of the mountains.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: Constrained ground limits expansion, while earthquake damage has required restoration. Both natural hazards and new construction affect the relationship between town and bay.

takeaway: Shelter at sea can come with very little room on land.

name: Valletta
title: A peninsula became a planned fortress city.
deck: Valletta concentrated streets, institutions, and defences between two harbours.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Valletta’s story?
options: An inland basin in the Himalayas
A settlement without any coastal access
A peninsula between two harbours

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: The peninsula between Grand Harbour and Marsamxett Harbour offered an elevated site with water along both sides. Its shape created a narrow but strategic building area.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: The Order of St John developed a fortified capital with an organised street plan. Public buildings, churches, and defensive works filled a compact area rather than spreading across a broad plain.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: Limited space and changes in level make access a design problem. A living capital must accommodate daily movement within an unusually concentrated historic landscape.

takeaway: A planned city can still take its essential shape from the coastline.

name: Naples
title: A coastal city kept building on its past.
deck: Naples’ historic centre carries the imprint of successive Mediterranean cultures.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Naples’s story?
options: A Mediterranean bay with successive urban layers
A settlement founded on Antarctic ice
A city with no connection to the sea

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: The Bay of Naples places the city beside the sea, with higher terrain behind its dense neighbourhoods. The waterfront offers connections while slopes influence expansion.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: Greek settlement and later societies left successive layers of streets, buildings, and institutions. The historic centre preserves traces of these different periods within a continuing city.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: A long-lived centre is not a single frozen plan. Conservation must work with everyday housing, movement, and the needs of a densely inhabited place.

takeaway: Naples is a palimpsest: later urban life has kept writing over earlier foundations.

name: Avignon
title: A riverside town became a seat of power.
deck: Avignon’s monumental skyline reflects an exceptional period in its history.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Avignon’s story?
options: A capital built on a coral reef
A Rhône crossing reinforced by papal institutions
A city founded at the Amazon estuary

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: The Rhône offered a major river corridor. The bridge and fortified town linked movement along the water with routes reaching its banks.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: The fourteenth-century papacy made Avignon a centre of religious and political authority. The palace, surrounding institutions, and city walls gave that role a lasting architectural presence.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: Political importance can move elsewhere while buildings remain. The city now cares for a monumental inheritance whose scale reflects a particular historical moment.

takeaway: Geography offered a location; an institutional decision transformed its importance.

name: Toledo
title: A river loop framed a hilltop city.
deck: Toledo’s compact setting holds layers of changing political and cultural life.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Toledo’s story?
options: A floating city in the Baltic
A settlement on an unbroken flat desert grid
A hill framed by a loop of the Tagus

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: The Tagus curves around steep ground supporting the historic city. Approaches and crossings make the difference between being surrounded by water and being connected across it.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: Successive Roman, Visigothic, Islamic, and Christian authorities shaped Toledo. Jewish, Christian, and Muslim communities contributed to a complex architectural and cultural inheritance.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: A striking defensive setting also constrains movement. Historic streets and steep approaches need care as present-day uses occupy an inherited urban fabric.

takeaway: Toledo’s ground helps explain its outline, while its history explains the layers inside.

name: Córdoba
title: A riverbank became a centre of authority.
deck: Córdoba combines a Guadalquivir crossing with a remarkable history of urban patronage.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Córdoba’s story?
options: The Guadalquivir crossing and successive centres of power
A harbour on the Pacific Ocean
A settlement with no river connections

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: The Guadalquivir provides a clear river edge beside the historic centre. A bridge connects the banks and channels movement towards the old city.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: Córdoba became a major centre under Islamic rule. Later Christian institutions adapted and added to the city, including the cathedral within the former Great Mosque.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: Different periods overlap in the same buildings and streets. Understanding the city requires reading those changes rather than assigning the whole place to one era.

takeaway: A useful river site becomes distinctive through the institutions people build around it.

name: Granada
title: Two hills held different faces of a city.
deck: The Alhambra and Albayzín face one another above Granada’s lower town.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Granada’s story?
options: A city built entirely on a lagoon
Opposing hills above a river valley
A plain without changes in elevation

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: Adjacent hills divided by the Darro valley create strong changes in level and opposing views. The lower city lies beneath these elevated historic districts.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: The Alhambra developed as a fortified palace complex, while the Albayzín grew as a residential quarter. Gardens and water systems formed part of a carefully adapted urban landscape.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: Steep terrain gives the city dramatic views but complicates access. Preserving the hillsides and their relationship is part of caring for the architecture.

takeaway: Granada’s famous views are relationships between places, not just isolated monuments.

name: Fez
title: A valley became a dense urban world.
deck: Fez’s medina grew around water, movement, commerce, and institutions.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Fez’s story?
options: A remote coral island
A capital constructed on permanent sea ice
A river valley with a dense network of urban institutions

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: The historic city occupies a valley setting crossed by waterways. Slopes and watercourses helped shape a compact fabric of lanes and neighbourhoods.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: Successive rulers and communities developed mosques, schools, markets, fountains, and lodging for merchants. Marinid patronage gave many important monuments their surviving form.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: Dense historic streets do not easily accommodate every modern service. Conservation must support residents and working neighbourhoods alongside the care of monuments.

takeaway: A city is sustained by everyday networks as much as by its celebrated buildings.

name: Marrakesh
title: A capital gathered routes and people.
deck: Marrakesh’s importance grew through political foundations and connections across a wider region.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Marrakesh’s story?
options: An inland centre connected by regional land routes
An Atlantic island harbour
A settlement at the source of the Danube

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: An inland plain near the Atlas Mountains offers a different setting from Morocco’s coastal ports. Connections here depended on routes across land rather than an urban seafront.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: Founded by the Almoravids in the eleventh century, Marrakesh became a political, economic, and cultural centre. Walls, gates, gardens, and public spaces expressed that role.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: An inland city needs more than a convenient meeting point. Its water, gardens, buildings, and busy public spaces require sustained management as uses change.

takeaway: A city does not need a seaport to become a powerful regional crossroads.

name: Zanzibar City
title: A coastal town connected cultures.
deck: Stone Town’s streets and buildings reflect a long history of Indian Ocean exchange.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Zanzibar City’s story?
options: A pass through the Rocky Mountains
Indian Ocean maritime connections
A city in a landlocked Arctic basin

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: Zanzibar’s island setting opened towards sea routes linking East Africa with other Indian Ocean shores. The waterfront connected the town to movement across water.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: Swahili urban traditions interacted with influences from the Arab region, India, and Europe. Trade and political change left their marks on buildings and the street pattern; this history also includes slavery and exploitation.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: A historic port is also a place where people live. Maintaining homes, infrastructure, and buildings matters alongside presenting its trading history.

takeaway: Connections leave cultural traces, but their human consequences must also be remembered.

name: Hội An
title: A trading port left its street plan behind.
deck: Hội An preserves the urban fabric of a port shaped by local and overseas exchange.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Hội An’s story?
options: A city on a polar ice sheet
A settlement without any waterway access
A river port linked to maritime trade

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: The Thu Bồn river system connects the town with the coastal region. Water access helped make an inland riverbank part of a wider maritime network.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: From the fifteenth to nineteenth centuries, the town developed as a trading port. Local building traditions and overseas influences combined in houses, assembly halls, and a distinctive street plan.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: Commercial functions can shift while a townscape survives. The challenge is keeping the old fabric inhabited and usable rather than treating it only as scenery.

takeaway: A port’s trading role can change while its connections remain visible in the streets.

name: Luang Prabang
title: Two rivers framed a royal town.
deck: Luang Prabang’s peninsula holds a distinctive meeting of urban traditions.
question: Which setting or connection best helps explain Luang Prabang’s story?
options: The meeting of the Mekong and Nam Khan
The delta of the Nile
A town built in an empty volcanic crater

steps.label: THE LANDSCAPE
steps.title: Read the ground.
steps.text: The Nam Khan meets the Mekong beside the historic town. Water on two sides defines a narrow site with hills contributing to its wider setting.

steps.label: THE HUMAN CHOICE
steps.title: People gave the setting a purpose.
steps.text: Royal and religious institutions shaped traditional Lao urban life. Later colonial buildings introduced another architectural layer without erasing the town’s earlier structure.

steps.label: THE TRADE-OFF
steps.title: A useful setting still needs care.
steps.text: New development must fit more than individual monuments. Riverbanks, street patterns, homes, and religious places together create the town’s character.

takeaway: A confluence can frame both a settlement and the encounters recorded within it.
